At a Glance

This is the second video in the CampusX Agentic AI using LangGraph playlist. Where Video #1 motivated Agentic AI by walking through its evolution from chatbots, this one does the formal study: a precise definition, the six traits that make a system agentic, and the five components every agentic system contains internally.

The lecture is intentionally theoretical — its goal is to plant the vocabulary you'll need for the rest of the playlist, where the same concepts will reappear inside actual LangGraph code. Reading these notes alongside short revision sessions is enough to internalise the framework.

What you'll learn

  • A formal definition of Agentic AI and how it contrasts with reactive chatbots.
  • A concrete walk-through of an HR recruiter agent that ties every concept to behaviour.
  • Six characteristics: autonomy, goal-orientation, planning, reasoning, adaptability, context-awareness.
  • Five high-level components: Brain (LLM), Orchestrator, Tools, Memory, Supervisor.

1. What is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI is a type of AI that can take up a task or goal from a user and then work towards completing it on its own, with minimum human guidance. It plans, takes actions, adapts to changes, and seeks help only when necessary. In simple terms: you provide a goal, and the system figures out how to achieve it — handling planning and execution itself.

1.1 Reactive vs. autonomous — the Goa-trip example

A reactive chatbot like ChatGPT only answers what you ask. If you want to plan a Goa trip, you keep asking question after question — best transport? best hotels? where to eat? — and the bot answers each one in isolation. The planning happens in your head.

An agentic AI works differently. You give it one goal — "Plan my Goa trip from the 15th to the 18th" — and it autonomously figures out the transport, hotels, attractions, and itinerary. The human is looped in only for approvals.

2. Concrete Example — The HR Recruiter Agent

To make the abstract concrete, picture an HR recruiter at a company that has built an agentic AI assistant. The recruiter's task: hire a remote backend engineer with 2–4 years of experience. Instead of running the entire pipeline manually, they hand the goal to the agent.

2.1 What the agent does, end-to-end

  • Understands the goal and forms a plan internally: draft JD → post → monitor → screen → interview → offer → onboard.
  • Drafts a JD by reading company documents (stack, salary band, responsibilities); shows it for approval.
  • Auto-posts the JD on LinkedIn and Naukri using their APIs.
  • Continuously monitors application count. If only two people apply in three days, it diagnoses the problem and proposes adaptations: broaden the JD to full-stack, run paid ads on LinkedIn. Asks for permission, then executes.
  • When applications arrive, it parses résumés and ranks them — strong / partial / weak.
  • Schedules interviews against the recruiter's calendar; mails invites; sends a reminder on the day with a question bank.
  • Drafts an offer letter, sends it via email, monitors for the reply.
  • On acceptance, triggers onboarding: welcome mail, IT access, laptop provisioning, intro meeting.

The striking feature of this example is autonomy. The recruiter gave one goal; the agent did the planning, the execution, and the in-flight adaptation by itself, looping the human in only at decision points.

3. The Six Characteristics of an Agentic AI System

If someone shows you an AI system and asks whether it qualifies as agentic, these are the six traits to check. All six should be present.

3.1 Autonomy

Autonomy is the ability to make decisions and take actions on its own to achieve a given goal, without needing step-by-step human instructions. This is the single biggest trait: in the recruiter example, the agent received one goal and then planned, executed, and adapted by itself.

Autonomy shows up in three places

  • Execution autonomy — the agent walks through plan steps without asking the user to advance each one.
  • Decision autonomy — choices like "how many candidates to shortlist" are made by the agent itself.
  • Tool-use autonomy — given many tools, the agent decides which one to use and when.

Why autonomy must be controlled

Unbounded autonomy is dangerous. An agent could roll out offer letters with wrong salaries, screen candidates with hidden bias, or spend unlimited money on ads. So autonomy is always constrained in practice.

Four ways to control autonomy

  • Scope Permission scopes — limit which tools and actions the agent can perform independently.
  • HITL Human-in-the-loop checkpoints — require human approval before high-risk steps (e.g., posting to LinkedIn).
  • Override Override controls — let the user pause, stop, or change the agent's behaviour at any time.
  • Rules Guardrails and policies — hard rules the agent must follow (e.g., "never schedule interviews on weekends").

3.2 Goal-Oriented

Being goal-oriented means the agent operates with a persistent objective in mind and continuously directs its actions to achieve it, rather than just responding to isolated prompts. The goal is the compass that gives autonomy its direction — without a goal, autonomy has nowhere to point.

Independent goals vs. constrained goals

  • Independent: "Hire a backend engineer."
  • With constraints: "Hire a backend engineer who is based in India", or "...within a $10,000 spend", or "...remote only."

How goals are stored — a conceptual representation

Goals live in the agent's memory as structured data. Different libraries store them differently, but conceptually it looks like this:

{
  "main_goal": "Hire a backend engineer",
  "constraints": {
    "experience": "2-4 years",
    "remote": true,
    "stack": ["Python", "Django", "AWS"]
  },
  "status": "active",
  "created_at": "2024-09-01",
  "progress": {
    "jd_drafted": true,
    "posted_on": ["LinkedIn", "Naukri"],
    "applications_received": 8,
    "interviews_scheduled": 2,
    "offer_sent": false,
    "onboarding_done": false
  }
}

Goals can be altered mid-way

If you decide partway through that you'd rather hire a freelancer than a full-time engineer, you can change the goal. The agent's plan and execution adjust to match the new goal — no need to start over.

3.3 Planning

Planning is the agent's ability to break down a high-level goal into a structured sequence of actions or sub-goals, and then choose the best path to achieve the desired outcome. Many practitioners consider this the most important characteristic: agentic systems essentially run a Plan ↔ Execute loop, and the quality of the plan determines the quality of the outcome.

Planning is a search problem

From an initial state ("company needs a backend engineer") to a goal state ("backend engineer hired"), there are many possible paths. The agent must choose the path that's most efficient and best aligned with constraints — exactly like a search problem.

How planning runs internally — three steps

  • Step 1 — Generate multiple candidate plans, not just one. For hiring, Plan A might be "post on LinkedIn + Naukri + AngelList" and Plan B might be "internal referral + hiring agency."
  • Step 2 — Evaluate each plan against criteria: efficiency (how fast?), tool availability (do we have it?), cost, risk of failure, alignment with constraints.
  • Step 3 — Select the best plan via a built-in scoring policy, hard-coded rules, or human-in-the-loop confirmation. Then move to execution.

3.4 Reasoning

Reasoning is the cognitive process through which an agent interprets information, draws conclusions, and makes decisions — both while planning and while executing. A simple human analogy: your phone gets stolen → you interpret what your environment is telling you → you draw the conclusion that the thief might misuse your number → you decide to call the carrier to block it. That is reasoning, and agents perform exactly the same kind of process.

Where reasoning is needed during planning

  • Goal decomposition — splitting a goal into sensible sub-goals.
  • Tool selection — figuring out which tool fits which step (e.g., "to find the salary band, I need Google search").
  • Resource estimation — judging time, dependencies, and risk.

Where reasoning is needed during execution

  • Decision-making — when multiple options appear (e.g., "interview 2 candidates or all 3?").
  • Human-in-the-loop judgment — knowing when to ask for help vs. self-serve via search.
  • Error handling — when LinkedIn's API is down, do you retry, escalate, or switch platforms?

3.5 Adaptability

Adaptability is the ability to modify plans, strategies, and actions in response to unexpected conditions while staying aligned with the goal. In the recruiter example, when the agent noticed application traffic was low after three days, it adapted: broaden the JD to full-stack and run a paid ad.

Three triggers for adaptation

  • Tool failures — the calendar API is down, so the agent switches to messaging the user directly to ask for availability.
  • External feedback from the environment — too few applicants, weather change, blocked ad budget, etc.
  • Goal change mid-way — the user changes the brief; the agent re-plans accordingly.

3.6 Context-Awareness

Context-awareness is the ability to understand, retain, and use relevant information from the ongoing task, past interactions, user preferences, and environmental cues to make better decisions across a multi-step process. Hiring takes days — without retaining context, the agent would forget what JD it posted and which candidates it has shortlisted.

What sits in an agent's context

  • Original goal — always available, never forgotten.
  • Progress so far + the chat history with the human supervisor.
  • Environment state — "job is live on LinkedIn, 8 applicants so far, ad budget runs out in 2 days."
  • Tool responses — "Candidate B has 3 yrs Django + AWS", "calendar shows Friday is free at 2 PM."
  • User preferences — "this recruiter likes question banks delivered in Google Docs."
  • Policies and guardrails — "never send an offer letter without explicit approval."

Context lives in memory

Implementation of context-awareness uses memory. Agents typically have two kinds of memory, mirroring how humans do:

  • Short-term memory — anything tied to the current session: tool responses, immediate decisions, chat turns.
  • Long-term memory — high-level goals, user preferences, guardrails, decisions that persist across sessions.

4. The Five Core Components of an Agentic AI System

Almost every LLM-based agent you'll meet has five high-level components inside it. More can exist — and each one can be subdivided — but at this introductory level these five are enough to map any agentic codebase you read.

4.1 Brain (LLM)

In LLM-based agents, the brain is a Large Language Model. It does most of the heavy cognitive work: interpreting the user's goal, planning a sequence of steps, reasoning at each decision point, picking which tool to use, and producing natural-language responses for the user. In other agent paradigms (e.g., reinforcement learning) the brain is a different kind of model, but throughout this series we focus on LLM-based agents.

4.2 Orchestrator

The orchestrator is the project manager. It executes the plan that the brain produced — running step 1, branching to step 2 or step 3 based on the result, retrying when a tool fails, and looping when needed. It's typically what your agent framework provides for you (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, etc., all give you orchestrator primitives).

What the orchestrator handles

  • Task sequencing — deciding what runs in what order.
  • Conditional routing — branching based on intermediate outputs.
  • Retry logic — when a tool fails or a service is down.
  • Looping and iteration — repeating steps until a condition is met.
  • Delegation — handing tasks to humans or to other agents/tools.

4.3 Tools

Tools are how the agent interacts with the external world. Anything outside the LLM that the agent calls — APIs, databases, parsers, the calendar, an HRMS, even a RAG knowledge base — is a tool. Tools are the agent's hands and feet.

Crucially, a RAG retrieval pipeline counts as a tool: it's how the agent grounds its answers in factual or domain-specific information.

4.4 Memory

Memory implements context-awareness. It stores both ephemeral and persistent information so the agent can reason across many steps and across many sessions.

  • Short-term — current-session messages, tool calls, immediate decisions.
  • Long-term — high-level goals, past interactions, user preferences, decisions made across sessions.
  • State tracking — "what have I already done? what's still pending?"

4.5 Supervisor

The supervisor is the human-in-the-loop component. It glues the human and the agent together so they can collaborate safely. Its main jobs:

  • Approvals for high-risk actions (e.g., sending an offer letter, running paid ads).
  • Enforcing guardrails — making sure the agent never violates the policies set on it.
  • Handling edge cases — if the agent finds something unusual that doesn't fit its rules, the supervisor escalates to the human.

5. Quick-Reference Summary

5.1 The six characteristics — checklist form

# Characteristic What it means How it shows up
1AutonomyActs without step-by-step human instructionsAgent posts the JD, screens résumés, schedules interviews itself
2Goal-OrientedPersistent objective drives every actionAll actions traced back to "hire backend engineer"
3PlanningBreaks goal into sub-goals, picks best pathGenerates Plan A and Plan B, evaluates, selects
4ReasoningInterprets info, draws conclusions, decidesDetects low-traffic JD, picks correct tool
5AdaptabilityRe-plans when reality changesBroadens JD when applications are too few
6Context-AwareRemembers the goal, progress, prefs, toolsRemembers what was posted three days earlier

5.2 The five core components — checklist form

# Component Role Analogy
1Brain (LLM)Interprets goal, plans, reasons, picks tools, writes languageThe thinking organ
2OrchestratorSequences tasks, routes, retries, loopsThe project manager
3ToolsExternal APIs, RAG, parsers, calendar, mailHands and feet
4MemoryStores short-term + long-term contextThe agent's mind
5SupervisorHuman-in-the-loop approvals, guardrails, escalationsThe safety officer

6. Why This Matters for the Rest of the Series

Everything in this video is theoretical, but it's the vocabulary you need before reading any agentic codebase. When you implement an agent in LangGraph, you'll explicitly create nodes that map to the brain (LLM call), the orchestrator (graph edges and conditional routing), the tools (tool nodes), the memory (state objects), and the supervisor (human-feedback nodes).

The six characteristics are the design goals — every well-built agent should be auditable against this list. The five components are the structural pieces — every well-architected agent should be decomposable into these layers.

If a system has all six characteristics, it is agentic. If you can name its five components, you understand its architecture.
